title: Glory on the Mountain, Failure in the Valley
summary: On a high mountain Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, Moses and Elijah appear with him, and a voice from the cloud calls him the beloved Son. Below, the other disciples have failed to free a boy from a spirit, and Jesus heals him after his father's desperate prayer. Jesus predicts his death a second time, the disciples argue about who is greatest, and he teaches them about childlike greatness, generosity toward other workers, and the seriousness of sin.
story: Six days after Peter's confession and the first prediction of the cross, three disciples are given a glimpse of the glory that lies beyond it. The transfiguration answers the question the book has been asking, now from heaven itself: this is God's beloved Son. But the chapter will not let the disciples stay on the mountain. They come down into a crowd, an argument, a suffering child, and their own powerlessness. Then Jesus repeats the prediction of his death, and they respond by arguing about rank. The pattern set in chapter 8 continues: prediction, misunderstanding, teaching. The disciples keep hearing about glory and missing the road to it.
historical:
Mark does not name the mountain. Christian tradition from about the fourth century identified it with Mount Tabor in lower Galilee, while many modern scholars favor Mount Hermon, the high mountain near Caesarea Philippi where chapter 8 was set. The text says only that it was high and apart.

The scribes' teaching that Elijah must come first rests on Malachi 4:5-6, the last words of the prophetic books in the Christian Old Testament, where God promises to send Elijah before the great and dreadful day of the Lord to turn the hearts of fathers and children. Jewish hope in Jesus' day expected Elijah's return to prepare for God's final act. Jesus affirms the expectation and says it has already been met in John the Baptist, whom they have done to as they wished, a reference to his execution by Herod Antipas in chapter 6. The word Gehenna (translated hell) is the Greek form of the Hebrew name for the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where some kings of Judah had sacrificed children by fire (2 Kings 23:10, Jeremiah 7:31). The prophets made it a picture of judgment, and by Jesus' day it had become a name for the place of final punishment. The common idea that it was a burning rubbish dump is attested only much later and is doubted by many scholars.
cultural:
The shelters Peter wants to build are the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles, the autumn festival when Israel lived in temporary huts to remember the wilderness years and looked ahead to God's final dwelling with his people. Peter may be trying to make the glorious moment permanent. The cloud recalls the cloud of God's presence that covered Mount Sinai and filled the tabernacle, and the voice's command, listen to him, echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promised a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear.

The boy's symptoms (seizures, foaming, rigidity, falling into fire and water) resemble what we would call epilepsy, and Matthew's parallel uses a word for being moonstruck, the ancient term for that condition. Mark presents it as the work of a spirit, and Jesus addresses the spirit directly; the Gospels treat illness and demonic oppression as distinct but sometimes overlapping. Children in the ancient world had little status, and taking a child in his arms as the representative of himself was a startling act. The millstone of verse 42 is the large kind turned by a donkey, far heavier than a household hand mill. Salt was used to preserve food and was added to sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13), which may lie behind the saying that everyone will be salted with fire.
literary: The chapter moves down a mountain in more than one sense. The transfiguration (verses 2 to 8) is followed by a conversation on the descent about resurrection and Elijah (9 to 13), and then by the story of the boy, which is told at length and full of dialogue. The father's cry, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” is one of the most honest prayers in Scripture. From verse 30 the scene shifts to teaching in Galilee and Capernaum, gathered as a series of sayings linked by catchwords: in my name (verses 37 to 41), little ones and stumbling (42 to 47), fire (48 to 49), and salt (49 to 50). This was a common way of arranging remembered sayings. Verses 44 and 46 are absent from the earliest manuscripts; they repeat verse 48 and were likely added by copyists. Some manuscripts add and fasting in verse 29.

outline.t: Some will see the kingdom come with power
Coming down the mountain: resurrection and Elijah
The boy with an unclean spirit and his father's faith
Who is the greatest: the child in Jesus' arms
The outsider who casts out demons in Jesus' name

doctrines.note: The Father's voice from the cloud names Jesus his beloved Son, repeating the words of the baptism (1:11). The transfiguration reveals the glory that belongs to the Son, a glory the church confesses as his by nature, not borrowed.

The father's prayer shows that faith is not the absence of doubt but trust that brings its unbelief to Jesus. The disciples' failure is linked to prayer (verse 29), which is faith turned toward God rather than toward one's own power.

Jesus speaks of Gehenna with language from Isaiah 66:24 and urges drastic action against sin. The images of cutting off a hand or plucking out an eye are hyperbole, not instructions for self-harm, but they teach that final judgment is real and that nothing is worth keeping at the cost of entering life.

Greatness in the kingdom means being last of all and servant of all, and welcoming the smallest in Jesus' name. The kingdom also has wider borders than the disciples assumed: whoever is not against us is for us.

words.note: Metamorphoo, to be transformed or changed in form. The word describes a change that shows outwardly what is true inwardly. Paul uses the same verb for believers being transformed by the renewing of the mind (Romans 12:2) and into the Lord's image (2 Corinthians 3:18). Here the glory is Jesus' own, briefly visible.

Geenna, Gehenna, from the Hebrew name of the Valley of Hinnom. In the New Testament it is almost always on Jesus' lips and names the place of final judgment, distinct from Hades, the realm of the dead. Jesus uses it to warn his own disciples, not only outsiders.

Diakonos, servant, one who waits on others, especially at table. The word later came to name an office in the church (deacon), but here it is the calling of every disciple. Jesus defines greatness by it and will describe his own mission with the related verb in 10:45.

Apistia, unbelief or lack of trust. Jesus laments an unbelieving generation (verse 19), and the father confesses his own unbelief and asks for help. The same word described Nazareth in 6:6. Mark shows that unbelief can be refused, as in Nazareth, or confessed, as here, and the difference matters.

christ: On the mountain Jesus is revealed as the beloved Son whose glory, usually veiled, belongs to him. Moses and Elijah, representing the Law and the Prophets and both men who met God on a mountain, speak with him and then disappear, leaving Jesus alone as the one to be heard. He is the prophet like Moses promised in Deuteronomy 18, and more than a prophet. But the chapter holds glory and suffering together: the transfiguration is followed immediately by talk of rising from the dead, the Son of Man who must suffer, and a second prediction that he will be delivered into the hands of men. The glory on the mountain is a preview of the resurrection, and the one who lifts the boy who looked like a corpse will himself be raised.

hard.q: What did Jesus mean when he said some standing there would not die before seeing the kingdom of God come with power?
hard.a: Verse 1 has been read in several ways. Many interpreters, ancient and modern, connect it with the transfiguration that immediately follows: within days, three of those standing there saw the kingdom's glory displayed in Jesus. Others see it fulfilled in the resurrection and the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost, when the kingdom came with power in a way the disciples witnessed. Some link it to the destruction of the temple in AD 70, within the lifetime of many of Jesus' hearers, as a visible act of judgment and vindication. A number of critical scholars read it as a prediction that the final coming of the Son of Man would happen within that generation, and conclude that it was not fulfilled; defenders of the other views answer that Mark himself placed the saying directly before the transfiguration, which suggests he saw it as fulfilled there, and that Mark 13:32 shows Jesus refusing to fix the date of the end. The first three readings are not exclusive, and many interpreters see the transfiguration as a foretaste of what the resurrection and Pentecost made public.

questions: The father prayed, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” What unbelief would you need to bring honestly to Jesus if you prayed that prayer today?
The disciples argued about greatness right after hearing Jesus predict his death. Where do you notice yourself measuring rank or importance, even in church?
John wanted to stop someone who was doing good in Jesus' name but was not one of them. How do you respond to Christians outside your own circle or tradition?
